subject: Post-call recap: pricing nexus — requests vs tokenization vs caching
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
To: Sophie Lang <sophie.lang@acme.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-05-11T15:03:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call recap: pricing nexus — requests vs tokenization vs caching

Hi Sophie — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick recap and a couple of clarifying bullets so we don't mix terms across teams: 

Summary of what I heard from the call:
- Primary workload: reranking + multi-turn customer summarization for shipments (batch and interactive).
- Target throughput: ~1M–4M tokens/month across both loads (rough estimate today's call).
- Budget framing: team mentioned a comfort zone around a target of roughly $2–$4 per 1M tokens, but wanted to confirm how caching/requests affect that.

Where confusion usually comes up (how we define terms):
- "Token" = model tokenizer unit (what our billing counts). For English conversational text, ballpark conversion is ~4 characters per token (varies).
- "Character" counts are not the billing unit — they’re a rough way to estimate token volume when you only have raw text.
- "Request" = a single API call. Some customers think "requests" and "tokens" are interchangeable — they are not. Requests are a count of calls; tokens are compute/usage per call.
- "Prompt caching" = reuse of a cached KV-prefix on the serving side. If a prefix is served entirely from cache, we do not re-run that compute and you are not billed for those cached input tokens (you are billed for the tokens the model computes on — i.e., the uncached input tokens + generated output).

Concrete example to make math easy:
- Full prompt length: 800 tokens (includes a 300-token reusable system prompt + 500-token per-request customer text)
- If the 300-token prefix is served from prefix cache, billed tokens for that call = 500 input tokens + generated tokens (e.g., 200 generated) = 700 billed tokens.
- If price = $2.50 per 1M tokens, cost per that call = (700 / 1,000,000) * $2.50 = $0.00175.

Notes on request-based or per-call pricing: we can offer hybrid pricing for high-request volumetry (e.g., reranking endpoints) where there is a small fixed per-request component and a token component. That structure helps when many calls are very short (few tokens) and per-token alone understates operational overhead.

Attached: Redwood_Pricing_Examples.xlsx — I populated quick line items with the above example and a couple of scenarios (no cache vs 50% prefix reuse vs 90% reuse).

Next steps — quick asks for you so we can give a tighter pilot estimate:
1) Can you share a 3–7 day sample of actual request traces (timestamps, request token counts, response token counts)? acme_sample_traces.csv would work.
2) Which model family are you targeting for pilot (lighter Llama-family, or higher-quality LLM)? That drives the per-1M price band.
3) Are you targeting a per-month price cap (e.g., $5k/mo) or a per-1M token target (e.g., $3/1M)? We can map either to expected throughput.

If helpful, we can run a short 2-week pilot with monitoring of effective billed tokens and cache hit rates so you can see real unit economics before committing to Dedicated.

Thanks — copying Aditya and Marissa for any engineering/CS follow-up.

Best,
Mina Haddad
Enterprise Sales 
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: pricing nexus — requests vs tokenization vs caching

Hi Sophie — answers inline and with a couple of quick charts (see attached workbook):

1) Cache billing behavior (hosted vs Dedicated):
- Hosted API: we support prefix/KV caching at the platform level for many customers; cached prefix serving reduces billed tokens in hosted deployments when the cache hit is at inference time. That said, caching guarantees depend on request routing and model variant selection. For the strongest cache guarantees (cold-start-free prefix warmers, pinned model instances), Dedicated gives more predictable cache hit behavior.

2) Hybrid per-request pricing for reranking:
- When request size is very small (50–150 tokens), per-request overhead (networking, scheduling, small-kernel overhead) can make pure per-token pricing less favorable. In those cases we offer a hybrid: small fixed cents-per-request (e.g., $0.0003/request) + lower per-1M-token price. The math typically shows savings when median tokens/request < ~200 and request QPS is high. We can model this for your traces.

3) Budget mapping ($3k/month example):
- Scenario A (no prefix cache): assume average billed tokens/call = 250, calls/day = 6k -> monthly tokens = 250 * 6000 * 30 ≈ 45M tokens. At $2.50 per 1M => ~ $112.50/month (wait that arithmetic is off — correcting below).
- Corrected worked example (explicit):
  * If you have 6,000 calls/day and average billed tokens/call = 250 -> monthly tokens = 6,000 * 250 * 30 = 45,000,000 tokens.
  * At $2.50 / 1,000,000 tokens -> monthly cost = (45,000,000 / 1,000,000) * $2.50 = 45 * $2.50 = $112.50 (this is per 1M token math; double-checking units).

(Note for finance: 45M tokens at $2.50/1M is $112.50 — if your spreadsheet shows larger numbers, it may be because it assumes tokens are reported in characters or in thousands rather than absolute tokens; we can reconcile once we ingest your trace.)

4) Practical mistakes we see when teams estimate costs:
- Using characters instead of tokens without applying the tokens-per-character factor (~0.25 token/character) leads to 3–5x errors.
- Confusing request counts with token counts (lots of short requests with per-request add-on can shift economics).
- Not accounting for generated tokens (summaries or assistant responses) in billed tokens.

Next steps I recommend (short list):
- We’ll import acme_sample_traces.csv and run a 7-day cost projection for: no-cache / moderate-cache (50% prefix reuse) / high-cache (90% prefix reuse).
- If you want hybrid pricing modeled, tell us the acceptable per-request floor (e.g., $0.0003) and we’ll show a side-by-side.
- If finance truly needs a $3k/month hard cap, tell us and we’ll produce an expected tokens/month and likely degradations (reduced QPS or truncation) that would be required.

I’ll assign Aditya to ingest the CSV and run the projection — Aditya, can you take that offline and post the projection to the HubSpot deal + the Drive folder linked above?

Best,
Mina
